Operator: Good morning, and welcome to the Pinnacle Energy Corp. Q2 2024 Earnings Conference Call. All participants will be in listen-only mode. After today's presentation, there will be an opportunity to ask questions. [Operator Instructions] As a reminder, this conference is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the conference over to Alex Rivera, Head of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Alex Rivera: Thank you, operator, and good morning, everyone. Welcome to Pinnacle Energy Corp.'s Q2 2024 Earnings Call. Joining me on the call today are CEO Ramirez, Chief Executive Officer; Sarah Jenkins, Chief Financial Officer; Lisa Chen, Chief Operating Officer; Mark Thompson, Chief Strategy Officer; Dr. Elena Vasquez, Chief Technology Officer; Robert Kline, Chief Regulatory Officer; and Jennifer Hale, Chief Communications Officer.

Before we begin, I'd like to remind you that statements made during this call that are not historical facts are forward-looking statements and are subject to risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to differ materially from those expressed or implied. Please refer to our SEC filings for a detailed discussion of these risks.

Now, I'll turn the call over to CEO Ramirez.

CEO Ramirez: Thank you, Alex, and good morning, everyone. I'm pleased to report on our performance this quarter. We continued to execute on our strategic priorities, delivering solid results in a challenging environment.

Our performance was driven by:
    1. Retirement of fossil fuel plants and replacement strategies.
    2. Earnings guidance for the next quarter and full year.
    3. Forward-looking statements and implications.
    4. Revenue breakdown by regulated and unregulated segments.
    5. Storm response and recovery efforts.
    6. Investments in renewable energy and clean energy transition.
    7. Management's perspectives on industry trends and challenges.
    8. Positive regulatory outcomes and enhanced community engagement.

Let me provide some more detail on these eight key aspects. Starting with our retirement of fossil fuel plants and replacement strategies, as well as several of the financial elements, I'll turn it over to Sarah Jenkins, our CFO, to walk us through those in depth.

Sarah Jenkins: Thank you, CEO Ramirez, and good morning, everyone. As we review our Q2 results, I'd like to dive deeper into one of our core strategic pillars: the orderly retirement of our legacy fossil fuel fleet and our comprehensive replacement strategies. This initiative is central to our long-term decarbonization goals, aligns with evolving regulatory frameworks like the EPA's Clean Power Plan 2.0 and state-level mandates such as California's SB 100, and positions us to capitalize on the plummeting levelized cost of energy—or LCOE—for renewables, which have fallen to around $25-35/MWh for utility-scale solar and $30-45/MWh for onshore wind, per recent Lazard analyses—now 40-60% below new-build combined-cycle gas turbine builds.

Let me start with the facts on our fossil retirements. Over the past 12 months, we've successfully decommissioned 450 MW of subcritical coal capacity at our Mid-Atlantic Basin facility in PJM, ahead of schedule and under budget at $120 million in total decommissioning costs, including asset retirement obligations or AROs. This brings our cumulative coal retirements to 1.8 GW since 2020, representing 35% of our legacy coal portfolio. Looking forward, we plan to retire an additional 1.2 GW of coal and 800 MW of simple-cycle gas peakers by the end of 2028, timed to coincide with the expiration of our current power purchase agreements—or PPAs—and capacity performance auctions in PJM and MISO. These retirements will reduce our fossil fuel exposure from 28% of our total 15 GW capacity mix today to under 15% by 2030, delivering annual fuel and O&M savings of approximately $250 million, which directly accretes to EBITDA at a 25-30% margin.

Economically, this makes perfect sense. Our remaining coal units are operating at capacity factors below 40%, hammered by $4-6/MMBtu natural gas prices and $50-70/ton carbon pricing signals emerging in RGGI states. Post-retirement, we're booking a one-time non-cash impairment of $350 million this quarter, but that's more than offset by $180 million in avoided variable O&M and a 15% uplift in our forward capacity auction revenues from cleaner resources.

Now, turning to replacement strategies—the real value creator here. We're not just shutting down; we're repowering smarter and faster. In Q2, we energized 650 MW of solar PV plus 200 MW/800 MWh of four-hour lithium-iron-phosphate battery storage at our former coal site in ERCOT, leveraging co-location to minimize transmission upgrades and secure $75/kW-year ancillary service payments. This hybrid project, developed with NextEra Energy Resources, achieved a post-tax IRR of 12.5% and is already dispatch-optimized via our proprietary AI-driven EMS, or energy management system, yielding 95%+ availability during peak summer loads.

Our pipeline is robust: 2.3 GW of renewables and storage under construction, with 4.8 GW in late-stage interconnection queues across PJM (1.2 GW), ERCOT (2.1 GW), and SPP (1.5 GW). Key initiatives include:

Solar + Storage Hybrids: 1.5 GW slated for 2025-2027, tapping 30% ITC adders under the Inflation Reduction Act. In the Southwest, we're mirroring Southern Power's model with First Solar Series 7 thin-film panels paired with Tesla Megapack 2XL enclosures, targeting 50% capacity factors in high-DNI regions like Arizona.

Offshore Wind Repower: A 400 MW allocation from our recent BOEM lease in the New York Bight, using GE Vernova Haliade-X 13 MW turbines. This addresses Northeast reliability gaps post-Indian Point nuclear retirement, with PPAs at $70/MWh blending PTC and state renewable portfolio standard—or RPS—credits.

Gas Transition with Abatement: For baseload needs, we're retaining 1.5 GW of efficient CCGTs with hydrogen-readiness uprates, including 20% H2 blending pilots akin to Intermountain Power Project. We're also advancing CCUS on 300 MW, targeting 90% capture rates with $85/ton 45Q credits, though economics hinge on sustained $50+/ton CO2 markets.

Regionally, this plays out differently. In PJM, where coal retirements have accelerated 25% YOY per monitoring analytics, we're focusing on fast-ramp storage to capture FTR uplift—financial transmission rights—and RPM capacity prices averaging $150/MW-day. ERCOT's pure energy-only market favors our 1.2 GW battery portfolio for ERCOT's ORDC—obligation resource curtailment demand curve—yielding $200+/MWh scarcity pricing spikes, as seen in last summer's heat domes. In the West under WECC, hydropower variability from drought is driving our 500 MW wind repowers in the Columbia Gorge, integrated with Idaho Power-style demand response programs.

Strategically, this fleet transition enhances our resource adequacy metrics, with ELCC—or effective load-carrying capability—for our new solar-storage at 45-60% versus 10-15% for standalone solar. We're hedging via 70% fixed-price PPAs and REC offtake, locking in 10-12% ROE on $4.2 billion capex through 2030, funded 60% equity, 40% green bonds at 4.2% yields. Risks? Interconnection delays—we've derisked with 80% approved queues—and supply chain for bifacial modules, mitigated via long-term offtakes with Qcells.

In summary, our fossil retirement program isn't just compliance; it's a $1.5 billion NPV generator over the decade, driving EPS accretion of $0.45/share annually from 2026. We're on track for 80% carbon-free generation by 2035, ahead of peers like Duke Energy, and positioned for the utilities' golden era of renewables growth.

Turning now to earnings guidance, as we wrap up a solid second quarter, where we delivered adjusted EPS of $1.42—up 8% year-over-year—and generated $2.85 billion in revenue, beating our guidance midpoint on strong thermal dispatch in ERCOT and higher-than-expected renewable output in PJM, let me turn to our outlook for the back half of the year.

First, for Q3 2024, we are guiding adjusted EPS to the range of $1.55 to $1.65, with a midpoint of $1.60. This represents about 12% growth at the midpoint versus Q3 2023. Revenue is expected to come in at $2.9 billion to $3.0 billion, driven by seasonal peak demand from air conditioning loads across our Northeast and Texas footprints, where we anticipate wholesale prices in PJM to average $45-$55/MWh and ERCOT nodal prices north of $60/MWh during heat events.

Key drivers here include load growth: We're forecasting 4.2% year-over-year retail load growth in our regulated utilities, fueled by data center additions—we've already signed 450MW of new load commitments from hyperscalers like Microsoft and Google under long-term PPAs at fixed rates above our weighted average cost of capital.

Generation mix: Our fleet utilization hits 68% in Q3, with gas-fired combined-cycle plants (CCGTs) at 75% capacity factor amid low Henry Hub prices hovering around $2.50/MMBtu. Renewables contribute 28% of output, up from 24% last year, thanks to the full-quarter ramp of our 350MW Brazos Valley solar farm in Texas and 150MW of battery storage in PJM, which captured $25 million in ancillary services revenue from frequency regulation.

Headwinds to flag: O&M expenses up 5% quarter-over-quarter due to wildfire mitigation costs in California—similar to what PG&E reported last quarter—and higher property taxes. We also factor in a $0.03 EPS headwind from interest expense on our recent $500 million green bond issuance for the Empire Wind offshore project.

On the full-year 2024 guidance, we are narrowing and raising our outlook across the board. Adjusted EPS is now $5.90 to $6.10, up from our prior range of $5.75-$6.05 and 10% above FY2023's $5.40. Adjusted EBITDA guidance tightens to $4.2 billion to $4.3 billion, implying 7-9% growth. Revenue remains at $11.6 billion to $11.9 billion, with free cash flow before growth capex at $1.8 billion to $2.0 billion.

This reaffirmation reflects several tailwinds materializing faster than anticipated: Renewable expansion: We're on track to add 1.2 GW of renewables and storage YTD, including the 400MW Desert Sun hybrid solar-plus-storage in the Southwest Power Pool (SPP). This positions us to meet 35% clean energy by year-end, ahead of our NY REV decarbonization targets, and unlocks $150 million in PTC/ITC tax credits under IRA guidelines.

Thermal reliability: Coal retirements elsewhere—like Talen's Susquehanna nuclear uprate—have tightened supply, boosting our 5.5 GW gas fleet's merchant margins by 15%. We've secured 80% of our 2025 capacity stack in PJM's BRA auction at $110/kW clearing prices.

Regulatory tailwinds: Favorable ROE outcomes in our recent rate cases—12.5% authorized in Texas and 10.75% in Pennsylvania—add $120 million to rate base earnings. We're also progressing CCUS pilots at our Limestone coal plant, eyeing 45Q credits that could yield $50 million annually once online in 2026.

Regionally: ERCOT (35% of earnings): Battery deployments mitigate curtailments, supporting 6% load growth from EVs and crypto mining resurgence. PJM (40%): Grid resilience investments post-Irma-like storms yield $80 million in performance incentives. CAISO/SPP (25%): Wildfire risks cap upside, but our 200MW hydrogen blending trials at Palomar peakers position us for CPUC's clean firm power mandates.

Strategically, we're accelerating our $8 billion five-year capex plan, with 60% allocated to clean tech: 2 GW renewables, 1 GW storage, and grid hardening via advanced conductors and synchrophasors. This supports our 6-8% EPS CAGR through 2028, targeting a 15% ROIC on growth investments amid electrification megatrends—U.S. power demand up 20% by 2030 per EIA forecasts.

Risks to monitor include prolonged nat gas volatility—if Henry Hub exceeds $3.50/MMBtu—or delays in FERC Order 2222 DER participation, which could shave $0.05 off EPS. That said, our conservative fuel hedging (70% through Q1 2025 at $2.80/MMBtu) and $2.5 billion liquidity provide a strong buffer.

Next, before I dive further into our forward-looking guidance and strategic outlook, let me remind everyone of our standard safe harbor statement. All statements made during this call regarding our future financial performance, operational results, capital deployment, and market opportunities constitute forward-looking statements within the meaning of the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995. These statements are based on current expectations, estimates, and projections, and are subject to risks and uncertainties, including but not limited to regulatory changes, commodity price volatility, supply chain disruptions, extreme weather events, and evolving demand from high-load growth sectors like data centers and EV infrastructure. Actual results may differ materially, and we undertake no obligation to update these statements except as required by law. Please refer to our SEC filings for a full list of risk factors.

With that, let's turn to our outlook for FY2025 and beyond, which underscores Pinnacle Energy Corp.'s positioned leadership in the evolving power generation landscape. We're guiding for consolidated adjusted EBITDA of $2.8 billion to $3.0 billion in FY2025, representing 8-12% growth over our FY2024 midpoint of $2.65 billion. This reflects a blend of regulated rate base expansion, merchant upside in our ERCOT and PJM exposures, and accelerating contributions from our clean energy portfolio, which now stands at 45% of our 28 GW total capacity—up from 32% just two years ago.

Key growth drivers and financial implications: First, renewables and storage scale-up. We're on track to commission 1.8 GW of new solar-plus-storage projects by year-end 2025, including our marquee 600 MW Desert Bloom facility in CAISO, backed by a 15-year PPA with a hyperscaler tech client at a weighted average contract price of $55/MWh—well above the California's REC-adjusted proxy. Battery storage additions total 1.2 GWDC / 4.8 GWh, leveraging our proprietary PinnacleFlow energy management software, which has already optimized dispatch revenues by 22% in our existing 800 MWh fleet through AI-driven arbitrage in real-time markets. We expect these assets to deliver an initial blended IRR of 12-14%, with long-term levelized cost of energy (LCOE) compressing to $28-32/MWh as panel costs stabilize post-2024 supply chain normalization. Capex for this queue is pegged at $2.2 billion through 2026, funded 60% via tax equity partnerships under IRA Section 45X/48E incentives, preserving our balance sheet leverage at 3.8x net debt-to-EBITDA.

Second, nuclear optimization and SMR pilots. Amid the nuclear renaissance—fueled by DOE loan guarantees and bipartisan support in the ADVANCE Act—our 2.4 GW legacy fleet at Three Rivers and Prairie Wind stations is targeting a 95%+ capacity factor in 2025, up from 92% this year, through uprates and extended dry cask storage approvals from the NRC. We're allocating $450 million in FY2025 capex for digital I&C upgrades akin to those at Vogtle Units 3&4, which should boost output by 150 MW equivalent. More excitingly, our 300 MW NuScale VOYGR SMR demonstration project in the MISO Midwest hub breaks ground Q4 2025, with commercial ops in 2028. This positions us for 2-3 GW of SMR deployments by 2030, tapping into baseload demand from AI data centers—projected by EIA to add 45 GW nationwide by 2030. We model nuclear contributing 25% of our EBITDA by FY2028, with FCF yields north of 10%.

Regional dynamics and merchant tailwinds: Regionally, our diversified footprint shines. In ERCOT, where load growth hit 5.2% YoY in Q2 amid heat domes and crypto rebounds, our 3.5 GW gas-and-renewables portfolio captured $250/MWh peaks during July's Heat Storm Zeta, driving 35% merchant margin expansion. We see sustained scarcity premiums through 2026, with our 500 MW peaker conversions to hydrogen-ready FlexFuel turbines ensuring dispatch flexibility. Conversely, in PJM, FERC Order 2020 implementation favors our 1.2 GW interconnection queue priority, de-risking $1.1 billion in queued solar/wind. Northeast exposure benefits from NY REV decarbonization mandates, where our 400 MW offshore wind stake with Ørsted mirrors Vineyard Wind's success, targeting 12% unlevered returns.

In the regulated West—PGE and Avista territories—rate base grows to $28 billion by 2026 via $1.5 billion annual capex, with ROE recovery to 10.2% post-Wildfire Fund contributions. Inflation pass-throughs and decoupling mechanisms shield us from volumetric risks as electrification accelerates: NREL forecasts 35% U.S. load growth by 2035, disproportionately in our service territories.

Strategic insights and risks: Strategically, we're prioritizing portfolio resilience through our "Clean Firm Power" thesis—blending intermittents with dispatchable zeros like geothermal (200 MW added via Fervo collaboration) and long-duration storage. M&A remains opportunistic; we've earmarked $800 million for bolt-ons, eyeing distressed thermal assets in SPP for conversion plays. Shareholder returns stay robust: $500 million in buybacks authorized, dividend payout at 70% of FCF, targeting 4.5% yield.

That said, headwinds loom. Natural gas basis volatility—Henry Hub forwards at $3.20/MMBtu—could pressure peaker margins if LNG exports surge. Supply chain delays on HVDC transformers, as seen with Siemens Gamesa's recent woes, risk 3-6 month queue slips. Regulatory scrutiny intensifies: CPUC's NEM 3.0 caps rooftop solar offsets, but our community solar programs mitigate via 20-year offtakes. Finally, extreme weather—IPCC models suggest 15% higher CAPEX intensity by 2030 for resiliency.

In summary, our FY2025 guidance embeds 7-9% EPS growth to $4.85-$5.15, with 2026-2028 CAGR of 10% driven by 15 GW clean queue execution and load growth. Pinnacle is uniquely leveraged to the trilemma of reliability, affordability, and decarbonization.

Good afternoon, everyone. As always, I'll walk you through the key financial drivers behind our strong results, starting with our revenue breakdown by regulated and unregulated segments. This bifurcation remains a cornerstone of our diversified business model, allowing us to deliver predictable cash flows from our regulated operations while capturing upside from our merchant activities in competitive markets.

For the quarter, we reported total revenues of $4.25 billion, up 6.2% year-over-year and exceeding our guidance midpoint by 2%. This performance was driven by a balanced contribution from both segments amid favorable demand tailwinds, including data center load growth and sustained industrial recovery. Weather was roughly neutral on a HDD/CDD basis, though we benefited from 3% higher residential usage tied to electrification trends.

Regulated Segment: $3.02 billion, or 71% of total revenues, up 4.8% YoY.

Our regulated utilities – spanning electric transmission and distribution in the Southeast (primarily SERC-NERC region, serving 4.2 million customers across Georgia, the Carolinas, and Florida) and Midwest (MISO footprint) – continue to anchor our stability. Revenues here grew on the back of approved rate cases, organic load growth, and recovery mechanisms.

Key drivers: Electric Distribution & Transmission: $2.45 billion (81% of regulated), up 5.2%. We earned a 9.75% ROE on our Georgia Power rate base following our successful 2023 general rate case, which added $180 million in annualized revenue. Transmission revenues benefited from FERC Formula Rate true-ups and higher network service investments under our $2.8 billion five-year capex plan, including 500 kV reconductoring projects to support 15 GW of queued renewables and hyperscaler interconnections.

AFUDC and Other: $570 million, reflecting constructive capitalization on our $1.1 billion quarterly capex, much of it in grid hardening post-Hurricane Idalia and battery storage pilots.

Regionally, Southeast volumes rose 4% on population-driven demand and EV charging infrastructure rollout, while Midwest transmission saw uplift from MISO's 2024 auction clearances at $45/kW-month average. We're on track for 3-5% CAGR through 2028, supported by state IRP approvals for 2 GW of new solar-plus-storage under the Inflation Reduction Act's ITC/SEIA extensions.

Unregulated Segment: $1.23 billion, or 29% of total revenues, up 9.5% YoY.

Our competitive generation and retail supply arms – operating 12 GW of merchant capacity across PJM, ERCOT, and SPP – delivered outsized growth, leveraging elevated spark spreads and capacity payments. This segment's higher volatility is managed through a disciplined 75% hedge profile for 2024-2025 output at $45-50/MWh forward strips.

Key drivers: Wholesale Power Generation: $890 million (72% of unregulated), up 12%. ERCOT real-time prices averaged $65/MWh, boosting margins on our 4 GW gas fleet (CCGT efficiency at 62% HHV). Nuclear output from our 1.8 GW Clinton station hit 95% capacity factor, capturing $75/MWh locational LBMPs in PJM amid summer peaks. Renewables contributed $220 million from 3.2 GWdc solar/wind portfolio, with PTC/ITC yields enhanced by IRA transferability – our recent 500 MW Texas battery co-location deal unlocked $150 million in monetized credits.

Retail Competitive Supply & Trading: $340 million, up 3%, driven by 1.2 million unregulated customers in deregulated states like Texas and Illinois. We grew margins via dynamic pricing algorithms and 20% YoY increase in REC trading volumes tied to compliance markets.

Trends here are promising: Unregulated EBITDA margins expanded 250 bps to 28%, fueled by data center PPAs (200 MW signed at $80/MWh fixed) and SPP capacity auction wins at $65/kW-year. However, we navigated Q2 headwinds like unplanned outages at our older coal units (now <5% of fleet), accelerating our retirement timeline to 2026 in line with EPA CSAPR updates.

Strategic insights and outlook: This 71/29 regulated-unregulated mix positions us uniquely – akin to peers like NextEra or Dominion – for resilient AFFO growth of 6-8% annually. We're prioritizing regulated capex at $10-12 billion over the next five years for T&D resiliency (e.g., AMI deployments reaching 90% coverage) and DER integration via our VPP platform, which aggregated 150 MW in pilots. Unregulated upside hinges on hedging efficacy and market betas; we've layered in 80% protection for 2026 at attractive levels, while pursuing 1 GW of hybrid renewables targeting 12-15% IRRs.

Looking forward, Q3 regulated revenues should grow 5% on seasonal billing and a pending Florida base rate proceeding. Unregulated expects 7-10% growth absent extreme weather, with full-year guidance affirmed at $16.8-17.2 billion total revenue.

Before moving on, I want to address our storm response and recovery efforts from Superstorm Elara, which made landfall across our Southeast and Mid-Atlantic footprints in late August. As you know, this was one of the most intense events we've faced in recent years, packing sustained winds over 120 mph, widespread flooding, and over 15 inches of rainfall in key service territories. It impacted approximately 2.8 million customers across our regulated utilities in North Carolina, Virginia, and South Carolina—representing about 40% of our total rate base exposure.

Our top priority, as always, was safety—for our employees, contractors, and customers—followed by rapid restoration to minimize SAIDI and SAIFI impacts. I'm proud to report that we executed one of our strongest responses to date, restoring power to 95% of affected customers within 72 hours and achieving full restoration across our system in under 10 days. For context, this outperformed our internal benchmarks and industry peers; Duke Energy reported a 5-day average restoration in similar 2022 events, while our SAIDI for the quarter came in at 180 minutes, well below the regional average of 245 minutes per EIA data.

Let me break this down operationally. Pre-storm preparations were critical. Leveraging our Advanced Distribution Management System (ADMS) from GE Grid Solutions, integrated with real-time weather modeling from The Weather Company, we proactively sectionalized 1,200 miles of high-risk distribution lines and deployed 450 automated fault indicators. This allowed us to isolate 65% of outages within the first 24 hours, compared to just 40% during Hurricane Fiona in 2022. We also activated our Storm Ready Centers in Raleigh and Richmond, staging 2,500 lineworkers, tree-trimmers, and vegetation management crews.

Response kicked off with mutual assistance mobilization under the Edison Electric Institute's (EEI) framework—we brought in over 4,000 external resources from 15 states, including PJM-interconnected partners like Dominion Energy and FirstEnergy. Drone patrols using FLIR thermal imaging covered 8,000 pole miles, identifying 1,200 downed structures and 15,000 snapped conductors before ground crews arrived, shaving an estimated 48 hours off initial assessments. In flood-prone areas like the Cape Fear River basin, we deployed 50 mobile substations and 200 portable generators, including Caterpillar C15 units rated at 500 kW each, to backfeed critical loads at hospitals and water treatment plants.

Recovery efforts shifted into high gear by Day 3. We prioritized Tier 1 customers—hospitals, 911 centers, and grocery chains—achieving 100% restoration there within 36 hours. By Day 5, residential restoration hit 92%, with commercial and industrial at 88%. Challenges included 350 transmission structures lost in coastal zones, where Category 4 winds toppled 138kV lattice towers, and underground cable failures in urban Charleston due to saltwater intrusion. We mitigated this with our fleet of bucket trucks equipped with ABB's SafeRing SF6-free switchgear for rapid reconfiguration, restoring 75 MW of load in under 4 hours per instance.

Regionally, North Carolina bore the brunt—1.9 million customers out, with 60% of outages from tree-wire contact in our rural Piedmont circuits. Virginia saw lighter wind damage but heavier flooding in the James River watershed, affecting 500,000 customers and delaying access for 72 hours. South Carolina's coastal exposure led to 400,000 outages, where we hardened 200 miles of lines post-event using concrete poles rated to 150 mph winds, drawing lessons from SCE&G's post-Hugo investments.

Financially, total storm costs hit $485 million, up 15% from our initial forecast due to extended vegetation management—$120 million on clearing 250,000 trees and limbs. Of this, $210 million was O&M expensed, impacting Q3 EPS by $0.18, already baked into our guidance. Capex of $275 million included $150 million for reconductoring 500 miles with ACCC conductors from CTC Global, which offer 2x capacity at half the sag—critical for our growing DER integration. Insurance recoveries are tracking at 85%, or $165 million net, with our $1.2 billion all-perils policy from FM Global covering 70% after deductibles. Regulated recovery via our formula rates—approved by the NCUC and SCC—will securitize 60% of unrecovered costs through storm bonds at ~4.5% yields, similar to Florida Power & Light's post-Irma mechanism. Expect $50 million in Q4 AFUDC credits as we capitalize these investments.

Strategically, Elara underscores the accelerating trend of extreme weather: NOAA data shows a 25% uptick in billion-dollar events since 2018, with utilities facing $150 billion in cumulative damages per ICF estimates. Our resilience capex has doubled to $1.8 billion over five years, targeting a 20% SAIDI reduction by 2025. Key initiatives include:

Grid Hardening: $400 million program deploying 10,000 smart reclosers from S&C Electric, enabling 30-second auto-restoration for 80% of momentary faults. Pilots in Virginia showed 15% fewer lockouts.

DER and Microgrids: Post-storm, we energized 50 community microgrids with Tesla Megapack batteries totaling 200 MWh, islanding 10,000 customers during peak outage hours. This integrates with our 1.2 GW solar portfolio, where Elara-tested inverters from Enphase held up flawlessly.

Vegetation Analytics: Partnering with Overstory.ai's LiDAR platform, we're optimizing $80 million annual trim cycles, reducing tree-related outages by 35% YTD.

Advanced Tech: Rolling out 500,000 AMI meters with Landis+Gyr's Gridstream, feeding AI-driven outage prediction models that flagged 70% of Elara's high-risk circuits 48 hours ahead.

Looking forward, we're raising our 2024 resilience budget to $2.2 billion, with 12% ROE hurdles under our multi-year rate plans. This positions us ahead of peers—our T&D capex intensity is 18% of rate base vs. S&P's utility average of 14%. Early modeling suggests every $1 invested in hardening yields $4-6 in avoided restoration costs, per Brattle Group studies. Customer satisfaction scores hit 92% post-Elara per J.D. Power, bolstering our regulatory goodwill.

As we dive into our strategic priorities, I'd like to spend a few minutes on our investments in renewable energy and the broader clean energy transition—a cornerstone of Pinnacle Energy Corp.'s long-term value creation strategy. In an industry facing accelerating decarbonization mandates, volatile commodity prices, and evolving grid dynamics, we've positioned ourselves as a leader in this space, leveraging our 50 GW regulated and contracted asset base to drive both growth and resilience.

Let me start with the numbers, which underscore our execution. Over the past five years, we've deployed approximately $12.4 billion in capital expenditures—or capex—into renewables and storage, representing 28% of our total capex during that period. In Q3 alone, we brought online 850 MW of utility-scale solar PV in the ERCOT market and 450 MW of onshore wind in MISO South, pushing our total renewable capacity to 18.2 GW as of quarter-end. That's up 22% year-over-year, with renewables now accounting for 42% of our overall generation mix—well ahead of the U.S. utility sector average of 28%, per EIA data.

Our return profile remains robust. These assets are delivering a blended ROE of 11.2%, supported by long-duration power purchase agreements—or PPAs—with investment-grade off-takers like Google, Amazon, and Microsoft under RE100 commitments. The average PPA tenor is 15 years, with pricing fixed at $35-45/MWh for solar and $28-38/MWh for wind, materially above the subsiding merchant prices in oversupplied markets like CAISO. Post-Inflation Reduction Act—or IRA—our effective tax equity yields have improved by 150-200 bps thanks to enhanced ITC and PTC transferability, allowing us to monetize credits without cumbersome partnerships.

Breaking it down by technology, solar remains our growth engine, comprising 55% of our renewable queue. We've shifted to high-efficiency n-type TOPCon modules from suppliers like First Solar and LONGi, achieving module efficiencies above 22.5% and DC/AC ratios optimized at 1.4-1.6x to maximize capacity factors in the 28-32% range across our Southwest fleet. A prime example is our 600 MW Gemini Solar + Storage project in Nevada, co-located with 380 MWh of four-hour lithium-iron-phosphate battery energy storage systems—or BESS—using Tesla Megapack 2XL units. This hybrid setup arbitrages peak DUOS pricing in the WECC, delivering $120 million in annual EBITDA at full dispatch.

Wind investments, at 30% of our renewables capex, focus on repowering legacy fleets with larger rotors and higher hub heights. In PJM, we've upgraded 400 MW of our Illinois wind farms with Vestas V150-4.2 MW turbines, boosting AEP by 15% to 45%. Offshore wind, while capex-intensive at $3,500-$4,200/kW, is a key pillar for our Northeast strategy. We're advancing 1.2 GW from our Empire Wind stake—acquired via our 2022 partnership with Equinor—targeting COD in 2027, with offtake secured via New York BQDM auctions at $110/MWh.

Storage is the linchpin of our transition playbook, with 1.8 GW / 7.2 GWh deployed or under construction—doubling our footprint YOY. Beyond lithium-ion, we're piloting flow batteries and long-duration tech like Form Energy's iron-air systems for 100-hour discharge in our PJM pilots, addressing duck curve challenges in California. These assets yield IRRs north of 14%, fueled by ancillary services revenue streams like regulation up/down and frequency response, which contributed 35% of Q3 storage EBITDA.

Regionally, our U.S. focus is bifurcated. In ERCOT, where load growth from data centers is exploding at 15% CAGR, we've secured 2.5 GW of solar + storage in the queue, capitalizing on negative pricing events to stack revenue from ERCOT's new ORDC market. Contrast that with the Northeast, where PJM capacity auctions cleared at $270/MW-day for 2025/26—our 1.1 GW portfolio there benefited from a 20% uplift. Internationally, our 15% stake in European assets via the Orsted JV gives us exposure to the EU's REPowerEU plan; we're investing €800 million in Baltic Sea offshore wind, hedging against TTF gas volatility amid the Ukraine crisis.

Strategically, this isn't just about adding gigawatts—it's about portfolio optimization and derisking. Renewables now hedge 65% of our thermal exposure, shielding EBITDA from Henry Hub swings; our gas fleet CCUS retrofits at $800/kW are progressing, with 20% CO2 capture online by year-end, qualifying for 45Q credits at $85/tonne. We're also at the forefront of grid-edge innovation, partnering with GE Vernova on hybrid gas-solar peakers and investing $250 million in dynamic line ratings—or DLR—to unlock 10-15% more renewable curtailment headroom.

Market tailwinds are aligning: BloombergNEF data shows solar LCOE has plummeted 89% since 2010 to $24-36/MWh unsubsidized, undercutting new-build combined cycle gas. Supply chain resilience is improving post-COVID, with U.S. polysilicon production ramping via First Solar's Series 7 factory. That said, we're not blind to headwinds—permitting delays under NEPA remain a drag, averaging 18 months for our federal land projects, which is why we've allocated $50 million to FAST-41 permitting accelerators. Intermittency risks are mitigated via 4-hour-plus storage co-location and AI-driven forecasting from our NextEra-sourced EMS platform.

Looking forward, our 15 GW development pipeline—valued at $45 billion—targets 60% renewables by 2030, with FY24 capex guidance of $4.2-4.6 billion, 65% allocated to clean energy. We expect this to accretively grow adjusted EBITDA by 8-10% CAGR through the decade, with FCF yield expanding to 7.5%. In a world where net-zero pledges from 70% of S&P 500 companies drive corporate PPA demand—up 25% YOY per LevelTen—we're primed to capture outsized returns.

Thank you, CEO Ramirez. Good morning, everyone. For the Q2, we reported earnings per share of $1.42 and revenue of $2.85 billion. Our financial performance reflects the strength of our diversified business model and our disciplined approach to capital allocation.

Our capital expenditure for the quarter was $650 million, primarily focused on renewable energy projects and grid modernization. We remain committed to maintaining a strong balance sheet and returning value to shareholders. We anticipate continued strong growth with our raised EPS guidance for the full year.

CEO Ramirez: Thank you, Sarah. Now, turning to management's perspectives on industry trends and challenges, as we wrap up our Q2 results, I'd like to spend a few minutes sharing our view on the broader Utilities and Power Generation landscape. We're navigating a transformative period in our industry—one defined by unprecedented demand growth, accelerating decarbonization, and persistent execution challenges. At Pinnacle Energy Corp., with our 25 GW diversified fleet spanning natural gas, nuclear, renewables, and emerging storage across the PJM, ERCOT, and SPP markets, we're uniquely positioned to capitalize on these shifts while addressing headwinds head-on.

Let's start with the tailwinds. Electricity demand is surging at rates we haven't seen since the post-WWII industrialization boom. U.S. EIA forecasts now project 4.7% compound annual growth through 2030, up from the 1.2% historical average over the past decade. Driving this are three megatrends: electrification, data centers and AI hyperscalers, and industrial re-shoring. EVs alone could add 1.2 million GWh of annual demand by 2035, per BloombergNEF, while hyperscalers like Amazon Web Services and Microsoft are signing 10-15 year PPAs for 20 GW of new capacity just this year—equivalent to 10% of ERCOT's peak load. In our Texas exposure, ERCOT summer peaks hit 85 GW in July, a 12% YoY increase, fueled by crypto mining rebounds and new semiconductor fabs from TSMC and Samsung.

On the generation side, renewables penetration is exploding. Solar capacity additions reached 32 GW in 2023—double 2022 levels—pushing the U.S. renewable share to 22% of the mix, per FERC Form 861 data. Wind held steady at 10%, but offshore wind is the wildcard: projects like Vineyard Wind and Empire Offshore off the Northeast coast are commissioning at 800 MW paces, with BOEM approvals accelerating for 30 GW by 2030. Battery storage is the enabler here—deployments jumped 75% YoY to 12 GW, with Tesla Megapack and Fluence systems achieving 90%+ round-trip efficiencies in our pilots. Capacity factors for solar have improved to 28% in sunny SPP markets thanks to bifacial panels and trackers, while our hybrid solar-plus-storage assets in Texas are delivering 50% higher IRRs at 12-14% versus standalone solar's 8-10%.

Regionally, the story varies. In PJM, where we have 40% of our fleet, load growth is tempered at 2.5% but constrained by retirements—over 40 GW of coal and gas slated to exit by 2032 under the EPA's Clean Power Plan 2.0. ERCOT remains the growth epicenter, with natural gas dispatch at 45% utilization amid 15 GW of new solar queueing up, but intermittency is biting: duck curve events now extend 6-8 hours daily. California, via CAISO, leads in storage mandates—8 GW online—but faces curtailment risks as rooftop solar floods the grid.

Now, turning to challenges, because no transition is frictionless. First, capex intensity: to meet net-zero by 2050, the sector needs $2.1 trillion in U.S. investments through 2030, per Wood Mackenzie—$110 billion annually, skewed 60/40 toward transmission and generation. Our own five-year plan calls for $8.2 billion, with $4.5 billion in renewables and $2.1 billion in grid hardening post-Hurricane Ida lessons. Elevated interest rates are compressing ROEs from 10% targets to 8.5% on new builds; a 100 bps Fed hike shaves 1-2% off unlevered IRRs for solar farms.

Supply chain bottlenecks persist: polysilicon prices for panels spiked 20% QoQ amid China export curbs, delaying 15% of our 1.2 GW solar pipeline. Turbine lead times for GE Vernova's 2.2-127 onshore units stretch to 36 months, exacerbated by IRA domestic content rules requiring 40% U.S.-sourced steel. Interconnection queues are a nightmare—FERC Order 2020 reforms notwithstanding, PJM's queue ballooned to 280 GW, with study delays averaging 4 years. We're advocating for MISO-style reforms to prioritize high-impact projects.

Regulatory and policy risks loom large. The Inflation Reduction Act's PTC/ITC extensions are a boon—yielding $1.2 billion in tax credits for our portfolio—but BEPS carbon border taxes could hit 5-10% on LNG exports, pressuring gas margins. Extreme weather adds volatility: 2024's Polar Vortex events drove 20% spikes in our hedging costs, while wildfires in SPP scorched 500 MW of transmission lines.

Strategically, we're leaning in. We've doubled down on 2.5 GW of battery storage co-located with our gas peakers, targeting 95% availability for ERCOT frequency regulation services at $50/kW-month premiums. Our nuclear uprates—mirroring Constellation Energy's playbook—added 150 MW at zero marginal cost, with SMR pilots from NuScale eyeing 77 MW deployments by 2028. On hydrogen, we're in DOE's Phase 2 hubs, blending 5% green H2 into our combustion turbines for 30% CO2 cuts without full retrofits. Digitally, AI-driven forecasting via Siemens Spectrum Power has cut our imbalance penalties by 25%, and we're piloting HVDC lines with ABB for 1,000 MW interconnections to unlock Midwest wind.

In summary, the industry is at an inflection point: demand outpacing supply by 150 GW through 2030 creates pricing power—our forward curves show $45/MWh in PJM vs. $30 last year—but execution risk is premium. At Pinnacle, our regulated ROE of 9.8%, investment-grade balance sheet, and 70/30 regulated-competitive mix give us resilience. We're guiding 6-8% EPS growth through the cycle, with renewables driving 15% EBITDA CAGR.

In ERCOT, we saw exceptional uplift from gas-fired peakers during the winter storm residuals and summer peaks, with realized heat rates averaging 45-48 $/MWh versus our forward strip of 42. Regulated recovery was solid at 30% or $250 million, primarily from our Midwest utilities arm with rate base growth to $18 billion, including 6% ROE authorized returns on new solar in MISO. Robert Kline: Sophie, regs are navigable. PJM MOPR: our solar qualified for full capacity credits at 85% ELCC—won our stakeholder vote last month, unlike some wind peers. ERCOT winterization: fully compliant post-'21 Uri, with $100M invested in dual-fuel backups; PUCT's new rules add minimal $20M opex. Coal: yes, retiring 1 GW Ohio subcritical by '26—replacing with 800 MW gas peaker + 400 MW storage hybrid, preserving 90% capacity value.

Portfolio: 45% renewables now (up from 35% '22), targeting 70% by 2030 via IRA ITC/PTC ($3B tax credits embedded). Net-zero '45 is feasible—leveraging existing nuclear (2 GW at 92% CF), CC efficiency, and CCUS pilots on 500 MW gas (DoE grant-funded). Vs. peers: cleaner than Vistra (60% fossil), on par with Dominion's renewables ramp, but our 20% merchant beta gives earnings torque. Risks? Supply chain—bifacial panels up 15% YoY cost—but locked 80% at $0.25/W.
